title: Matrix chain multiplication
text:
There are algorithms that are more efficient than the O(n3) dynamic programming algorithm, though they are more complex.

All are based on an equivalence (or reduction) between multiplication of n matrices, and triangulation of an n+1-sided regular polygon. The former consists of adding n−1 (correctly nested) pairs of parentheses to the product to give an order of evaluation, while the latter consists of adding n−2 non-intersecting internal edges to partition the polygon into n−1 triangles. In each case, the number of ways this can be done is Cn−1, the (n−1)-th Catalan number.

If the input matrices have dimensions wi−1×wi, we can construct an n+1-sided polygon whose vertices V0 through Vn are labelled with the corresponding dimensions w0 through wn. Each edge represents a matrix whose dimensions are the weights of its two endpoints: the n input matrices, and the final w0×wn product. For the purpose of visualization, imagine the final edge is the horizontal base at the bottom of the polygon, with the input matrices arranged clockwise above it.

A triangulation adds internal edges so that only triangles remain. Each triangle represents a multiplication which is performed, and each internal edge represents an intermediate product which is computed. The triangle including the base is the final product, and its two other edges are the multiplicands, which may be intermediate products at the bases of their own smaller polygons.

For the example below, there are four sides: A, B, C and the final result ABC. A is a 10×30 matrix, B is a 30×5 matrix, C is a 5×60 matrix, and the final result is a 10×60 matrix. The regular polygon for this example is a 4-gon, i.e. a square:

The matrix product AB is a 10×5 matrix and BC is a 30×60 matrix. The two possible triangulations in this example are:

The cost of a single triangle in terms of the number of multiplications needed is the product of its vertices. The total cost of a particular triangulation of the polygon is the sum of the costs of all its triangles:

(ABC: (10×30×5) + (10×5×60) = 1,500 + 3,000 = 4,500 multiplications

A(BC: (30×5×60) + (10×30×60) = 9,000 + 18,000 = 27,000 multiplications

The following 14 triangulations of a regular hexagon correspond to the 14 different ways that parentheses can be placed to order the multiplications for a product of 5 matrices.

### Hu & Shing

T. C. Hu and M.-T. Shing developed an algorithm[1,2,3] which finds an optimum solution for the minimum cost partition problem in O(n log n time. Their proof of correctness of the algorithm relies on "Lemma 1" proved in a 1981 technical report and omitted from the published paper.[4,2] The technical report's proof of the lemma is incorrect, but Shing has presented a corrected proof.[5]

### Other O(n log n algorithms

Wang, Zhu and Tian have published a simplified O(n log m algorithm, where n is the number of matrices in the chain and m is the number of local minimums in the dimension sequence of the given matrix chain.[6] That is, the number of positions at which wi < wi−1 and wi < wi+1 (subscripts computed modulo n+1).

### Chin-Hu-Shing approximate solution

An algorithm created independently by Chin[7] and Hu & Shing[8] runs in O(n and produces a parenthesization which is at most 15.47% worse than the optimal choice. In most cases the algorithm yields the optimal solution or a solution which is only 1–2 percent worse than the optimal one.[3]

The algorithm considers groups of three consecutive vertices V_{i-1}, V_i, V_{i+1} , along with the vertex V_\min with minimum weight w_\min .

We look at the quadrilateral with vertices V_\min, V_{i-1}, V_i, V_{i+1} (in clockwise order).

We can triangulate it in two ways:

(V_\min, V_{i-1}, V_i) and (V_\min, V_{i+1}, V_i) , with cost w_{\min}w_{i-1}w_i+w_{\min}w_{i+1}w_i

(V_\min, V_{i-1}, V_{i+1}) and (V_{i-1}, V_i, V_{i+1}) with cost w_{\min}w_{i-1}w_{i+1}+w_{i-1}w_{i}w_{i+1} .

If the latter is cheaper than the former, that is if

w_{\min}w_{i-1}w_{i+1}+w_{i-1}w_{i}w_{i+1} < w_{\min}w_{i-1}w_i+w_{\min}w_{i+1}w_i

or equivalently

\frac{1}{w_i}+\frac{1}{w_\min} < \frac{1}{w_{i+1}}+\frac{1}{w_{i-1}}

we remove the vertex V_i from the polygon and add the side (V_{i-1}, V_{i+1}) to the triangulation.

We repeat this process until no V_i satisfies the condition above.

For all the remaining vertices V_i , we add the side (V_\min, V_i) to the triangulation.

This gives us a nearly optimal triangulation.
